analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from forcing consumers and small businesses into arbitration over claims under federal and state laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Hank Johnson with 4 Democratic cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Federal Arbitration Act so that companies could no longer use fine-print clauses to force individuals and small businesses into private arbitration when they sue over violations of federal or state laws or constitutions. A person could still choose arbitration after a dispute arose, but could not be forced into it in advance, and a judge — not an arbitrator — would decide whether the arbitration clause was fair. It was a response to Supreme Court decisions like AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion that courts say have left millions unable to enforce their legal rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals and small businesses that have legal claims against companies — consumers, employees, franchisees, and borrowers. Today, when a contract contains a forced arbitration clause, those claims usually go to a private arbitrator instead of a court, and the fine print often blocks class actions, which is the only realistic way to challenge small-dollar wrongdoing. Under this bill, claims based on federal or state statutes or constitutions could be brought in court unless the person voluntarily agreed to arbitration after the dispute arose. Courts could also refuse to enforce arbitration clauses that state law deems unconscionable, restoring a tool that recent Supreme Court decisions had taken away from the states [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Lets individuals and small businesses take claims under federal or state statutes and constitutions to court instead of being locked into private arbitration by a contract signed before the dispute arose [S2] [S3].
Puts the question of whether an arbitration clause is enforceable back in a judge's hands, rather than letting the arbitrator — chosen and paid under the company's process — decide [S2] [S3].

Restores states' ability to protect their residents: courts could refuse to enforce arbitration agreements that state law treats as unconscionable or otherwise unenforceable, undoing the broad preemption the bill says came from Concepcion and Italian Colors [S3].

The bill's own findings state that these court decisions enabled businesses to avoid legal duties created by Congress, leaving millions of Americans unable to vindicate their rights in state and federal courts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that embed forced arbitration clauses in consumer, employment, and small-business contracts — banks, credit card issuers, telecom and cable companies, lenders, nursing homes, and large employers — would face lawsuits in open court, including class actions, for claims arising under statutes. Their arbitration providers would lose business. Some of those added legal costs could show up in prices or fewer services, and disputes would generally take longer and cost more to resolve than a single arbitration would.

drawbacks.text: Litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for many individual disputes, so some claimants with small, clear-cut cases might do worse in court than they would in arbitration.
Companies facing more lawsuits and class actions would bear higher legal costs, some of which could be passed on to customers in the form of prices or fees.

Critics of class actions argue they often deliver most of their value to plaintiffs' lawyers while consumers receive small payments; restoring court access would revive that channel, not guarantee larger recoveries.
The bill applies only prospectively, to disputes arising after enactment, so people already bound by existing arbitration agreements would get no relief [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: today, a forced arbitration clause can make a statutory right — against a payday lender, an employer, a cable company — practically unenforceable, because a private arbitrator decides and class actions are barred, and the bill's findings say millions of people are in that position [S3]. The costs are genuine but mostly fall on the companies being sued: more litigation, slower resolution, and possible price pass-through. Some honest trade-offs remain — individual arbitration can be cheaper and faster for simple disputes, and class actions do not always serve claimants well — but a person could still choose arbitration after a dispute arose, which preserves the voluntary version of the tool while removing the take-it-or-leave-it version. On balance the bill trades company convenience for access to the public court system.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee never took the bill up; it sat in a subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2017, so it never got a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on April 12, 2016, joined by Reps. Conyers, Chu, Jackson Lee, and Cicilline, all Democrats; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S3] [S5].
On April 28, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill drew only 4 cosponsors beyond its sponsor, never received a hearing or markup, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on forced arbitration clauses — banks, credit card issuers, telecoms, and large employers — are better off, because the Concepcion and Italian Colors framework they operate under stays fully intact and individuals and small businesses remain routed into private arbitration. Consumers and workers are left exactly where the bill's findings said they were: often unable to vindicate statutory rights in court.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its cosponsors

for.name: Reps. John Conyers, Judy Chu, Sheila Jackson Lee, and David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; Conyers was the ranking Democrat on the Judiciary Committee

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor action; after a routine subcommittee referral the bill sat untouched for the rest of the Congress

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and affected industries
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed limits on forced arbitration in consumer and employment contracts, defending the enforceability of arbitration clauses under the Federal Arbitration Act

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-run committee never acted; because the bill never reached a floor vote, no formal roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: These companies put forced arbitration clauses in standard account and loan agreements, which the bill would no longer let them enforce against statutory claims. Their interest lies in keeping disputes out of court and out of class actions, which runs against consumers' ability to enforce their legal rights.

Employment contracts routinely require workers to arbitrate claims under labor and civil rights statutes; the bill would let workers take those claims to court instead. Employers' interest in private, non-appealable dispute resolution runs against workers' access to the courts.

industries.industry: Telecom, cable, and other consumer-contract industries
industries.note: These industries use take-it-or-leave-it service contracts with mandatory arbitration; the bill would strip that shield for statutory claims. Their gain under the status quo comes at the direct cost of consumers' day in court.

Firms and associations that administer forced arbitrations would lose volume of mandatory cases, though voluntary post-dispute arbitration remains allowed. This is a smaller, secondary effect of restoring court access.
